intro: Woodworking machines for the cabinet shop, the joinery, the school shop and the serious home workshop. faq.q: Jointer, thickness planer or jointer-planer — what do I need?
faq.a: A jointer flattens one face of a rough board and squares an edge to it; a thickness planer then makes the other face parallel and brings the board to thickness. You need both to mill rough lumber. A jointer-planer (TDM) does both jobs with one cutterblock in the space of one machine — the tables lift for thicknessing — at the cost of a changeover between the two; separate machines are faster when both run all day.

faq.q: Spiral carbide cutterhead or straight knives?
faq.a: A spiral (helical) cutterhead has many small carbide inserts set in a spiral: it cuts with a shearing action, so it is quieter, leaves a cleaner surface on figured and interlocked grain and tears out less, and a chipped insert is turned to a fresh edge in a minute instead of a set of knives reground and reset. Straight knives cost less to buy and are fine for softwood and general work. The WJ jointers and WJP planers have spiral carbide heads; the WJ10X40 and the multifunction machines have straight knives.

faq.q: Which table saw — 30″ or 52″ rip, hand wheels or touch screen?
faq.a: The rip capacity is the widest cut to the right of the blade: 30″ is enough for solid wood and for cutting a sheet of plywood to 30″ parts; 52″ cuts a 4 × 8 sheet to any width, which a cabinet shop needs. All WTS10 saws take a 10″ blade with 3-3/8″ of cut at 90°; on the S models the blade height and angle are typed on a touch screen and shown digitally — faster and repeatable set-ups for production.

faq.q: Do I need a dust collector?
faq.a: Yes for every planer, jointer and table saw: they make chips faster than a shop vacuum can take them, and fine dust is a health risk. A single-stage collector like the DC900 — 940 CFM, two 4″ inlets — serves one or two machines at a time; keep the hose runs short and connect the machine that is running.

faq.q: What voltage do these machines run on?
faq.a: Three-phase machines are supplied for 600 V as standard with a CSA-approved panel; 208 V, 240 V and 480 V 3-phase are available on request, and 240 V single-phase on models with a small enough motor. Manual machines have no electrics.
